item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers’ roster gives opposing managers plenty to worry about, and WAR helps explain why. It also gives Dodger fans a reason to appreciate players whose contributions can get overshadowed by the biggest names on the marquee. Put hitting, pitching, defense and baserunning on a common scale, and the picture becomes more interesting than a collection of home run totals and earned run averages.
MLB’s projected playoff rosters rank Milwaukee first (53.7 WAR), Los Angeles second (52.0); Dodgers free-agent acquisitions account for 24.5. That makes for an intriguing October argument: how much should we trust the accumulated value of a roster when the season becomes a succession of short series?
First, it helps to understand what the number actually means.
WAR stands for Wins Above Replacement. It estimates how many additional wins a player contributes compared with a readily available replacement, such as a minor league free agent. A four-WAR player has provided roughly four wins beyond that baseline over his playing time. The comparison uses a standardized replacement level, rather than whoever happens to be sitting on his team’s bench.
For position players, FanGraphs combines batting, baserunning and fielding contributions, expressed in runs. It adjusts for position, league and ballpark, incorporates the replacement-level baseline, and converts those runs into wins. Roughly speaking, about 10 additional runs are worth one win, although the conversion varies with the scoring environment. Position matters because filling a demanding defensive assignment carries value that a batting line alone cannot capture.
Pitchers require a different calculation. FanGraphs starts with Fielding Independent Pitching, emphasizing strikeouts, walks, hit batters and home runs, with an adjustment for infield flies. It accounts for ballpark, innings and the different roles of starters and relievers, then converts performance above replacement into wins. Relievers also receive a leverage adjustment reflecting the situations in which they pitch. Consequently, a pitcher’s ERA and his WAR can tell somewhat different stories.
These are FanGraphs figures, commonly called fWAR. Baseball-Reference uses a different calculation, particularly for pitchers, so its totals can differ. WAR is also an estimate: a few tenths of a win should never end an argument about which player is better.
Here are the Dodgers’ leading contributors on the FanGraphs leaderboard:
| Player | 2026 Dodgers WAR |
|---|---|
| Shohei Ohtani | 6.6 |
| Yoshinobu Yamamoto | 4.7 |
| Andy Pages | 4.5 |
| Max Muncy | 4.2 |
| Mookie Betts | 3.7 |
| Freddie Freeman | 2.7 |
| Tanner Scott | 2.4 |
| Tyler Glasnow | 2.4 |
| Tarik Skubal | 2.2 |
| Justin Wrobleski | 1.9 |
| Blake Snell | 1.9 |
FanGraphs figures through the regular season, accessed September 29. Skubal’s entry reflects his Dodgers work.
Ohtani’s total combines 3.7 WAR as a position player with 2.9 on the mound. Yamamoto supplied his value across 185 innings. Pages and Muncy both cleared four wins, an excellent reminder to give them their share of the credit. Scott’s placement alongside Glasnow is striking, too, given how much less opportunity relievers generally have to accumulate value.
For October, the workload details deserve attention: Glasnow accumulated his total in 74 innings, Snell in 42⅔ and Skubal in 62 for Los Angeles. Their season totals describe what they contributed over those opportunities; a postseason rotation presents a different distribution of innings.
That is where I find the strongest argument for the Dodgers. A playoff team can concentrate its innings among its best available pitchers. If those arms are healthy and effective, the version of a club taking the field in October can be considerably more dangerous than its season-long totals suggest. The same principle works in reverse when an important contributor is unavailable.
I would take the Dodgers’ combination of options into any series with confidence. Having several plausible game-changers gives a manager room to respond when an opponent neutralizes one part of the roster. It also gives the lineup a chance to survive a quiet series from a star.
Still, picking Los Angeles over any individual opponent is a different proposition from picking it over the entire field. Every additional round creates another opportunity for a brilliant opposing starter, a costly mistake or a badly timed slump to decide things. WAR can help establish expectations; October still gets to write the results.
For Dodger fans, these numbers support optimism and an appreciation of how many players have helped put the club in this position. The roster has enough talent to make a championship a reasonable expectation. Turning that expectation into another parade remains the most difficult part.
More Dodgers Coverage:
Have you subscribed to the Bleed Los Podcast YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows & promotions, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!
A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.title: [MLB.com] Forever connected by Braves, Olson and Freeman welcome first postseason faceoff
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman
item.description: LOS ANGELES -- Freddie Freeman’s assumption that he would spend his entire career with Atlanta ended on March 14, 2022, the day the Braves acquired Matt Olson from the A’s. It was an awkward and initially painful separation for the man who had been the Braves’ everyday first baseman from 2011-2021. Needless to say, the pain has faded as Freeman has spent the past five years establishing himself as a legend in another organization. He’ll always cherish his days with the Braves. But over this next
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- Freddie Freeman’s assumption that he would spend his entire career with Atlanta ended on March 14, 2022, the day the Braves acquired Matt Olson from the A’s. It was an awkward and initially painful separation for the man who had been the Braves’ everyday first baseman from 2011-2021.
Needless to say, the pain has faded as Freeman has spent the past five years establishing himself as a legend in another organization. He’ll always cherish his days with the Braves. But over this next week, they will stand as the enemy.
Freeman’s Dodgers will face the Braves in the National League Division Series that begins on Saturday at Dodger Stadium. The 2020 NL MVP has played 29 games against Atlanta over the past five seasons. But this marks the first time he will face his original organization in the postseason.
“I understand it will be a storyline,” Freeman said. “I get it. But it is five years later. I'm not going to try and look at it any differently. It's another team that I'm trying to get through to win another championship.”
The NLDS will create another opportunity to highlight the link that will forever exist between Freeman and Olson, the two players who have combined to provide the Braves excellence at first base over the past two decades.
Freeman certainly didn’t like seeing his job given to somebody else. As for Olson, it wasn’t easy for him to come to Atlanta to replace a franchise icon. But never once has there been any sort of animosity or awkwardness between the two first basemen.
In fact, the two have attended events together, including a Morgan Wallen concert at Truist Park last year. There is a genuine mutual respect.
“Matt is a great guy and an unbelievable baseball player,” Freeman said. “He's one of the best power hitters in our game right now. So it's fun. And he's from [Atlanta]. That massive home run he hit yesterday was just cool.”
Olson’s 416-foot home run in the seventh inning of Thursday’s night’s 6-2 win over the Phillies reminded the baseball world of his great power. Atlanta’s first baseman ranks fifth among all MLB players with 329 homers since the start of 2018, his first full big league season.
With the 41 homers hit this season, Olson joined Hank Aaron (eight times), Eddie Mathews (four times) and Ronald Acuña Jr. (twice) as the only players to tally multiple 40-homer seasons for the Braves.
“Matt had a lot on his plate when he first got here,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “He was replacing an icon. I think we got the only guy that could do it, the only guy that could step in in that role at that time. Matt's been a superstar for us.”
The Braves’ final written offer to Freeman was a five-year, $135 million deal ($27 million average annual value). The 10-time All-Star was 32 at the time.
The Braves knew Freeman might have a few more MVP-caliber seasons in him. But they also were confident Olson would provide similar production through those first few years and then continue to provide elite production while Freeman moved north of 35.
Of course, Freeman holds the edge in batting average (.306 to .259), OPS (.885 to .852) and most importantly World Series titles (2 to 0) over these past five seasons. He highlighted this run by becoming the only player in MLB history to hit a walk-off homer in a World Series game multiple times.
Olson is still bidding for that big postseason moment. But more importantly, he’s vying to lead the Braves to a World Series title, just like Freeman did in 2021.
“I’d say he’s our captain,” Braves catcher Sean Murphy said. “He goes out there every single day and hit 40 home runs. I’d say we’re happy to have Matt Olson on our team."

item.title: [Chicago Tribune] Column: Can the Chicago White Sox keep succeeding in the postseason without a conventional rotation?
item.dc:creator: Paul Sullivan
item.description: CLEVELAND — If you’re a baseball fan of a certain age, you’ve probably spent most of your life knowing some certainties about a pitching staff. The five best guys (or four if you’re really old) are the starters who will try to get you through the bulk of the game. The best reliever is the closer, who pitches the last inning or possibly part of the eighth if he’s dominant enough. The next-best relievers — preferably one left-hander and one right-hander — are the setup men, the potential bridges f
item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND — If you’re a baseball fan of a certain age, you’ve probably spent most of your life knowing some certainties about a pitching staff.
The five best guys (or four if you’re really old) are the starters who will try to get you through the bulk of the game. The best reliever is the closer, who pitches the last inning or possibly part of the eighth if he’s dominant enough. The next-best relievers — preferably one left-hander and one right-hander — are the setup men, the potential bridges from starter to closer.
And the pitcher who is least effective on the staff is the mop-up man, whose main function is keeping the better relievers from being overused.
For years managers used that basic blueprint, or something close to it, to get through the regular season. Then when the playoffs arrived, the best three or four starters went longer because the season was almost over and they could empty their bullets in the biggest games.
But baseball has changed, for better or worse, and now anything goes. Boston Red Sox ace Sonny Gray was removed in the fifth inning of a do-or-die wild-card game Wednesday, and Gray and his teammates grumbled about how the game got to this point.
Which brings us to the 2026 Chicago White Sox, who are trying to win with a “no-rotation” rotation.
Will Venable, the second-year White Sox manager, announced Friday that left-handed reliever Hagen Smith would start Game 1 of the American League Division Series against the Cleveland Guardians, serving as the opener Saturday, as he did in pitching three scoreless innings in Game 1 of the wild-card win in Houston.
It’s no surprise. The Sox have used openers a league-leading 32 times this season, including Smith’s outing Tuesday. If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.
But does the no-rotation rotation have its limits, or can Venable’s Sox keep succeeding in the postseason with a bullpen-first strategy?
Venable acknowledged Sean Burke could start Game 2 on Monday, as he did in a four-inning start in Game 2 against the Astros, in which starters Anthony Kay and Erick Fedde both pitched in relief. But other than Burke, it might be a guessing game from here on out.
Can Smith come back to start Game 3 at home Wednesday, giving him three starts in their first five playoff games? Who knows what’s up Venable’s sleeve?
“I think the way it’s set up with these off days, we’re going to leverage the arms that we want to leverage when we want to use them throughout these first couple,” Venable said. “And if that means that one of the guys who we’ve been giving starts to throughout the season takes a bulk role in that, there’s certainly potential for that. But I think you can expect us to mix and match and use our best arms in the most optimal way.”
That suggests Smith and Grant Taylor can be the designated bookends of multiple games, with Jordan Hicks, David Sandlin and Sean Newcomb in the middle and Kay, Fedde and Davis Martin as the wild cards.
It’s almost the polar-opposite approach that then-manager Ozzie Guillén employed in the 2005 postseason, when José Contreras, Mark Buehrle, Freddy Garcia and Jon Garland combined for a 2.84 ERA in 12 starts, leading the Sox on an 11-1 run to their World Series title.
In the five-game win over the Anaheim Angels in the AL Championship Series, the four starters had four straight complete games and combined for 44 1/3 of the 45 total innings, with Neal Cotts contributing the other two outs in the ninth inning of the Game 1 loss. The rest of the bullpen had a nice seat to watch the starters dealing.
“I don’t know if you’ll ever see that again,” Sox catcher A.J. Pierzynski said afterward. “Managers just don’t do that anymore. They don’t have confidence to let guys go 120 pitches and throw nine innings.”
In the World Series, advance scout Bryan Little and his crew gave Guillén and pitching coach Don Cooper a near-perfect report on strengths and weaknesses of the Astros hitters. Contreras and Buerhle both went seven innings in the first two wins at Sox Park, and Garland went seven in Game 3 in Houston before the Astros tied it off Dustin Hermanson in the eighth.
Guillén was forced to use his well-rested bullpen when the game went 14 innings but also used Orlando “El Duque” Hernández and Buehrle. After Geoff Blum’s go-ahead home run in the 14th, Buehrle notched the infamous “buzzed save” by getting the final out after having a few beers in the clubhouse. “No more than three … I swear,” he later said.
Buehrle wound up on a Wheaties box, but he didn’t become a legend for his cereal-eating habits.
Game 4 was as old-school as it gets, with Garcia going seven shutout innings, Cliff Politte and Cotts getting the Sox through the eighth and Bobby Jenks closing out a 1-0 win to start the parade plans.
“That type of game is like the ones I watched for 162 games during the regular season,” Guillén said in the celebratory clubhouse.
Venable’s approach in the postseason also mirrors what he has done for much of the season.
General manager Chris Getz knew he didn’t have a dominant rotation in spring training, and opening-day starter Shane Smith was quickly dispatched to Triple-A Charlotte after three starts. Martin, Burke, Kay and Fedde have been the mainstays, though Fedde, who signed at the start of spring training, had only 15 starts in his 33 games.
Taylor has evolved into the de facto closer but can go three innings if needed. He also was used as an opener in April. Seranthony Domínguez led the team 12 saves, even after being dispatched at the trade deadline.
Openers aren’t a new concept. “Bullpenning” has been around for the last decade. Cubs manager Craig Counsell also used openers in last year’s postseason.
But is it possible no team has been as unconventional as the ’26 Sox in this particular run?
“It’s possible,” Getz said during the wild-card celebration. “We weren’t trying to re-create the wheel. We were trying to optimize the group that we had. So much of (baseball) has relied on starting pitching. We would’ve liked to do that. But if we were trying to win games, we had to lean on the strength of the club, and we’ve done that.”
The Sox’s strategy has been criticized, especially when an opener puts the bulk pitcher in a hole. Guillén himself has said on the Chicago Sports Network he’s not a fan of openers.
But if the Sox go all the way without a true rotation, the players may never have to buy a meal or drink in Chicago again. Or at least that’s the adage.
“More often than not I’ll just roll in and buy a drink or buy my dinner,” Blum told me last week in Houston. “But every so often, if there is a hard-core Sox fan in the bar or in the restaurant, there will be a free drink that will show up once in a while.”
So it’s kind of true?
“It still carries a little bit of weight,” Blum said. “We’re not quite the ’85 Bears, but the ’05 Sox do OK.”

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox might not have played well against the New York Yankees, getting swept in the Wild Card round by their biggest rival, but the series still made some history.
Whenever the Yankees and Red Sox play, especially in a playoff setting, it's typically action-packed, and fans watch from all over the world.
The Yankees and Red Sox are such big rivals because both organizations have strong teams year in and year out and are also massive brands.
According to the latest report, Game 1 between the two squads actually set some records, making it the most-watched opener of an MLB Wild Card or Division Series since 2006.
“Tuesday’s Game 1 averaged 7.3 million viewers across NBC and Peacock, making it the most-watched opener of an MLB Wild Card or Division Series since 2006, according to Front Office Sports. The rivalry gave NBC Sports a strong start in its return to postseason baseball,” Chris Spiering wrote.
Baseball continues to rise at a rapid rate, a very promising sign considering the potential lockout this offseason.
That's something owners don't seem to be considering right now, and it has to change.
For baseball to keep growing, a lockout right when the game is growing at this level would be very questionable. Not to say that the Red Sox and Yankees aren't a big reason for that, but baseball has also seen some upticks in other viewership numbers, and possibly ruining that would be a very bad sign.

item.content:encoded:
For the Sixth Consecutive Year, TelevisaUnivision’s Sports Audio Network Will Deliver Live, Play-by-Play Coverage of the MLB Playoffs Through the 122nd World Series Across All Platforms.
Courtesy: TelevisaUnivision
MIAMI, FL. – October 2, 2026 – TUDN Radio, the premier Hispanic sports audio network of TelevisaUnivision, will once again serve as the exclusive U.S. Spanish-language radio home for the 2026 Major League Baseball Postseason. Marking the network’s sixth consecutive edition delivering October baseball to Hispanic audiences across the nation, fans can experience the entire postseason journey entirely in Spanish—from the opening pitch of the Wild Card Series through the final out of the historic 122nd World Series.
Continuing its long-standing collaboration with Major League Baseball, TUDN Radio will bring every moment of the postseason to life, led by the voices of acclaimed announcers Luis Quiñones, Alberto “El Beto” Ferreiro, Daniel Alvarez, and Jesus Acosta. This elite broadcast team will provide unparalleled coverage across the network’s nationwide terrestrial radio footprint, as well as digitally via the Uforia app and TUDN’s digital platforms.
“Baseball holds a deep, passionate connection with our Hispanic audience, and we are incredibly proud to return for our sixth postseason as the exclusive Spanish-language audio voice of MLB,” said Carlos F. Azcarate, VP of Sports Radio Network. “We are thrilled to continue bringing fans closer to the diamond, delivering every pivotal moment, dramatic home run, and championship celebration directly to them, wherever they choose to listen.”
Unprecedented Coverage Across All Platforms
TUDN Radio will broadcast key matchups throughout each round of the postseason, culminating in comprehensive Spanish-language audio coverage of the entire Fall Classic. Listeners can tune in across multiple touchpoints:
- TUDN Radio Network: Broadcast across affiliate radio stations in primary Hispanic markets nationwide.
- The Uforia App: TelevisaUnivision’s audio platform, offering live streaming on mobile devices across the United States.
- TUDN.com and TUDN App: Live digital audio integration for fans following games online.
- Smart Speakers & Connected Devices: Voice-activated live streaming through supported home integrations.
The 2026 Postseason Schedule on TUDN Radio
TUDN Radio’s coverage will feature full pre-game, play-by-play, and post-game analysis across every round:
- MLB Wild Card Series: Complete coverage of the best-of-three opening rounds.
- American League and National League Division Series (ALDS & NLDS): In-depth coverage as teams battle for the pennant.
- American League and National League Championship Series (ALCS & NLCS): Live calls deciding the champions of each league.
- The 122nd World Series: Uninterrupted, full-series coverage of baseball’s championship showdown.
Adding to the comprehensive live game broadcasts, fans can catch all the surrounding excitement, expert breakdowns, and exclusive player interviews on TUDN Radio’s premier baseball show, Desde El Diamante.
Complete broadcast schedules, station directories, and talent assignments will be updated throughout the month as matchups advance. Fans can follow along with live game updates, highlights, and behind-the-scenes content on X, Instagram, and Facebook via @TUDNRadio and by visiting TUDN.com.
CONTACT:
Melissa Agudelo – Director of Communications, News & Sports
###

MIAMI, Florida – 2 de octubre de 2026 – TUDN Radio, la principal cadena de audio deportivo para la audiencia hispana de TelevisaUnivision, volverá a ser la casa exclusiva de radio en español en EE. UU. de la Postemporada de las Grandes Ligas 2026. Por sexto año consecutivo, la cadena llevará el beisbol de octubre a las audiencias hispanas de todo el país, permitiéndoles vivir de principio a fin la emoción de la postemporada en español, desde el primer lanzamiento de la Serie de Comodines hasta el último out de la histórica 122.ª Serie Mundial.
Como parte de su colaboración de larga trayectoria con Major League Baseball, TUDN Radio llevará a los aficionados cada instante de la postemporada de la mano de los reconocidos narradores Luis Quiñones, Alberto “El Beto” Ferreiro, Daniel Alvarez y Jesús Acosta. “El beisbol mantiene un vínculo profundo y apasionado con nuestra audiencia hispana, y nos llena de orgullo regresar por sexto año consecutivo como la voz exclusiva en español de la postemporada de la MLB”, afirmó Carlos F. Azcarate, VP de Sports Radio Network. “Nos entusiasma seguir acercando a los aficionados al diamante y llevarles cada momento decisivo, cada cuadrangular dramático y cada celebración del campeonato, sin importar dónde elijan escucharnos”.
Cobertura sin precedentes en todas las plataformas
TUDN Radio transmitirá los enfrentamientos más destacados de cada ronda de la postemporada, hasta llegar a una cobertura integral en audio en español de toda la Serie Mundial. Los aficionados podrán seguir la acción a través de múltiples plataformas:

- TUDN.com y la app de TUDN: Integración de audio digital en vivo para los aficionados que sigan los partidos por internet.
- Altavoces inteligentes y dispositivos conectados: Streaming en vivo mediante comandos de voz a través de las integraciones domésticas compatibles.
Calendario de la Postemporada 2026 en TUDN Radio
La cobertura de TUDN Radio incluirá previa, narración jugada a jugada y análisis posterior a cada encuentro durante todas las rondas de la postemporada:
- Serie de Comodines de la MLB: Cobertura completa de la ronda inaugural al mejor de tres juegos.
- Series Divisionales de la Liga Americana y la Liga Nacional (ALDS y NLDS): Análisis en profundidad mientras los equipos compiten por el campeonato de cada liga.
- Series de Campeonato de la Liga Americana y la Liga Nacional (ALCS y NLCS): Narración en vivo de los encuentros que definirán a los campeones de cada liga.
- 122.ª Serie Mundial: Cobertura ininterrumpida y de principio a fin de la gran batalla por el campeonato de las Grandes Ligas.
Además de las transmisiones en vivo de los partidos, los aficionados podrán disfrutar de toda la emoción alrededor de la postemporada, análisis especializados y entrevistas exclusivas con jugadores en Desde El Diamante, el programa insignia de beisbol de TUDN Radio.
Los calendarios completos de transmisiones, directorios de estaciones y asignaciones del talento se actualizarán durante el mes a medida que avancen los enfrentamientos. Los aficionados podrán seguir las novedades de los partidos en vivo, los mejores momentos y contenido exclusivo detrás de cámaras en X, Instagram y Facebook a través de @TUDNRadio, así como en TUDN.com.

item.title: [Sportsnaut] MLB Insider Claims Phillies Will 'Kick Around Idea' of Bryce Harper Trade This Winter: 5 Potential Landing Spots, Including the NY Yankees
item.dc:creator: Jasonburgosmma; Jason Burgos
item.description: After a disappointing end to the 2026 season, a prominent MLB insider believes the Philadelphia Phillies will consider trading long-time star Bryce Harper this winter. The Phillies entered this year with the fourth-highest payroll in MLB and big expectations. item.content:encoded:
After a disappointing end to the 2026 season, a prominent MLB insider believes the Philadelphia Phillies will consider trading long-time star Bryce Harper this winter.
The Phillies entered this year with the fourth-highest payroll in MLB and big expectations. While they didn’t win the National League East, the hope was that their talent-rich roster could still go on a deep run in the postseason. Unfortunately, despite their best efforts, Philadelphia came up short in their three-game Wild Card series against division rivals the Atlanta Braves.
Following their season-ending loss on Thursday, The Athletic’s Ken Rosenthal claimed, “The Phillies at least need to kick around the idea of trading” the All-Star first baseman. A player the MLB insider feels doesn’t have an “oppressive” contract, with five years and $118 million left on the deal.
If the team pulled the trigger on a trade for the two-time NL MVP this winter, here are five teams he could end up landing with this winter.
Chicago Cubs
The Chicago Cubs had an equally frustrating finish to their 2026 campaign this week as well. However, they didn’t even get to three games, and the team with the sixth highest payroll in baseball was soundly beaten by the San Diego Padres in just two.
Chicago could lose both of their corner outfielders this winter, so Harper could fill either of those spots. Or the nine-time All-Star could be an option at DH. Either way, Harper would be a really nice addition to the lineup. Plus, like Alex Bregman, he is a strong veteran leader and player in the postseason.
Boston Red Sox
The Boston Red Sox are another team that saw their playoff run ended in just two games. In their case, it was rivals the New York Yankees who eliminated them. Harper could certainly be an option for Boston at DH. But the thing this team lacks the most, which he would address, is a proven veteran leader on the field and in the clubhouse. If he can handle the pressure of Philadelphia, Harper would be fine in Boston.
Toronto Blue Jays
This season was a massive disappointment for the Toronto Blue Jays. After being a couple of outs away from winning the World Series last fall, the Jays finished dead last in the AL East with a 79-83 record this year. So you can bet they will look to make a big move this offseason to get back into title contention in 2027.
If the Phillies actually make Harper available in trade talks, Toronto will be fascinated by the idea of pairing him with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. next season. If Guerrero Jr. can return to the player he always has been in 2027, and Kazuma Okamoto puts up similar power numbers, adding Harper to the batting order gives Toronto a spot in the order you can’t pitch around.
New York Yankees
The Yankees are still in the race to be champions in 2026. However, if they fall short of that yearly goal, the Yanks will surely look into adding a piece or two that can get them to end their 17-year title drought.
New York would need to find a new home for Giancarlo Stanton, but with only one guaranteed season for $15 million left on his deal, it may be possible this offseason. If they can trade the injury-prone five-time All-Star, a lineup with a healthy Aaron Judge, Harper, Ben Rice, and Cody Bellinger is one of the best in baseball.
St. Louis Cardinals
While the St. Louis Cardinals finished 77-85 this season, they seemed a bit ahead of schedule in their rebuild because of the upside in young stars JJ Wetherholt and Jordan Walker. The Cards are willing to make bold moves for proven stars if they feel they can help get the team to the next level or change the culture for the better. Harper could do both.
With St. Louis having a top-five farm system in MLB, they would certainly have the prospect assets to easily get a deal done.

item.content:encoded:
The season for the Houston Astros came to an unceremonious close at the hands of the Chicago White Sox, who beat them two games to none in the MLB Wild Card Playoff round.
Now, the White Sox move on to face the divisional rival Cleveland Guardians in the Divisional Playoff round, while the Astros are left picking up the pieces and wondering where things went wrong.
Not long afterward, starter Hunter Brown expressed his frustration with how things turned out in a completely blunt recap.
Houston Astros Pitcher Hunter Brown Admits The Tough Truth After Series Loss To White Sox
Brown's start in Game 2 against the White Sox ended before the first inning was over, forcing the Astros to turn to their bullpen early. The Astros had already utilized eight pitchers during their Game 1 setback, and they also used six more in their regular season finale.
Brown faced nine Chicago batters, allowing five hits and four runs, three of which were earned. He also walked one batter and while also not getting much help from his teammates. The Astros committed a pair of costly errors, while Yordan Alvarez failed to catch a playable fly ball.
Ultimately, the White Sox picked up a 7-3 win, sweeping the Astros out of the playoffs and ending their dreams of another World Series run.
Afterward, Brown said that his performance wasn't up to snuff despite his best efforts.
"I feel like everything that could have went poorly did and I didn't overcome the whole inning, really," Brown said, per Brian McTaggart of MLB.com. "I felt like, looking back, it's hard to say I don't take anything back, but I feel like pitches that I threw I was confident and I threw them to the best of my ability. Just didn't come out on the right end of it. Unfortunately, that's the way it went, and they were able to slap a crooked number up there on the board."
A shoulder strain limited Brown's availability during the 2026 regular season, which saw him finish with a 3.19 ERA in 20 starts.
Hunter Brown Has Played His Entire MLB Career With The Astros
Brown was taken by the Astros in the fifth round (166th overall pick) of the 2019 MLB Draft. After making his professional debut that year, he missed the entire 2020 minor league season before moving through Double-A and Triple-A in 2021.
Brown broke out in 2022 with Triple-A Sugar Land, posting a 2.55 ERA and 106 innings while earning PCL Pitcher of the Year honors. His performance also made him Houston's top prospect and one of MLB's most highly regarded young pitchers.
Brown helped Houston win the 2022 World Series before becoming a full-time starter in 2023. After a strong second half in 2024, he broke out in 2025 with a 2.43 ERA, 206 strikeouts and his first All-Star selection.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Astros' Hunter Brown Admits Blunt Truth After Playoff Elimination appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [PhillyVoice] This era of the Phillies feels like it's over
item.dc:creator: Nick Tricome PhillyVoice Staff

item.content:encoded:
October 02, 2026
Ryan Howard twisted uncomfortably out of the batter's box, then crumpled just a few steps down the first-base line as the St. Louis Cardinals rushed toward the mound to celebrate.
An October-fueled Citizens Bank Park fell silent.
The Phillies had lost Game 5 of the 2011 NLDS, and suddenly, shockingly, their all-in chase after another World Series title was over.
Roy Halladay, with his last bit of true greatness, tossed a one-run gem that should've been enough of a chance, and yet was nullified by an even more brilliant complete game from Chris Carpenter, who made a Philadelphia lineup flush with high-profile bats look entirely pedestrian.
And then there was Howard at the end, the star slugger who was left lying there in the grass as the Phillies' grand ambitions all came crashing down.
No one wanted to say it out loud at the time. Maybe they just couldn't bring themselves to fully accept it just yet. But that image has since been permanently etched into the minds of every Phillies fan who witnessed it, because deep down, everyone knew right then and there: A golden era of Phillies baseball was over.
One by one, the generation defined by Howard, Jimmy Rollins, Chase Utley, Cole Hamels, that second-ever World Championship in 2008, and then Halladay, Cliff Lee, and any other big name that the organization could get its hands on in the pursuit of one more, faded.
Those Phillies were never competitive again.
Bryce Harper whiffed on a low and way, way away slider from Chris Sale that he never had a prayer of hitting, and that Drake Baldwin, behind the plate, never had a prayer of catching.
Harper, slowly and totally unaware, bent down to take his shin guard off, thinking it was strike three and that the inning was over. He never saw the ball spike past Baldwin in the dirt, and go rolling to the backstop. By the time he realized, all he gave was a disinterested jog up the first base line, which did finally end the eighth inning from Baldwin having the time to recover for the throw up to the base.
John Kruk: "RUN!"
Bryce Harper was slow to get out of the box, not realizing strike three had gotten away.
(Via: @MLB) pic.twitter.com/GRcx3VGWtQ
— Foul Territory (@FoulTerritoryTV) October 2, 2026
The Phillies were down, 6-2, in the deciding Game 3 of the 2026 NL Wild Card series, on the road against the rival Atlanta Braves.
They still had three outs of life left, but everyone watching knew full well – and probably had no hesitation admitting this time, just shy of 15 years later – that another playoff era of Phillies baseball was over.
And once this club does get back to South Philadelphia, there will be no World Series pennant to look up at in center field and over Ashburn Alley.
The closest this generation ever got was that first breakout run that burnt out against the Astros in 2022.
They only ever got further away from it from there, and now might be all out of chances.
The Phillies stood in the visiting clubhouse, and interim manager Don Mattingly sat at the press conference dais.
No one spoke with any certainties.
Mattingly, who took over midseason for Rob Thomson, talked around whether he wanted to come back and how he felt about the decision the Phillies will have to make this winter for whoever their next full-time manager is going to be.
"It's not the time to talk about anything like that," Mattingly said. "...I want the Phillies to do what they need to do."
Granted, anything shy of a World Series always seemed to point toward him not staying.
Alec Bohm, the first-round and homegrown infielder who was good but always had better expected of him, is now headed for free agency and didn't want to talk about what his future held either.
Trea Turner, who certainly will be back just by the nature of his enormous 11-year, $300 million contract, knows he can't with another season like this one, where his numbers at the plate are low and where you can never be fully confident that he'll properly field the baseball. That can't cut it.
"[I] got a lot of work to do," Turner said.
And then there was Harper, who didn't have much to offer either, save for one definitive statement.
"I'd imagine this team's gonna look a lot different next year," said Harper, "with the guys that are kind of leaving this clubhouse. We'll see."
If there even is a next year for baseball.
Either way, it does feel like this team has to be.
The next few weeks are undoubtedly going to put the Phillies and everyone responsible for their current construction up to harsh scrutiny, amid a fan base that, really, got tired of them two postseason failures ago.
Dave Dombrowski, the Phillies' president of baseball operations, will have the most to answer for, after he repeatedly ran it back with an aging core, failed once again to put together a competent bullpen, and ended this season with none of his trade deadline acquisitions on the postseason roster, all while presiding over a barren-looking farm system.
Hitting coach Kevin Long, who has long been immune from any other shifts in the dugout staff around him, has to face the music here, too, after the Phillies continued to have a collectively abysmal approach at the plate – outside of a month – and after seeing nearly all of the Phils' batters either plateau, regress, or in the case of Luis Arráez, to see a perennial .300-plus hitter suddenly drop well below that line the second he put on a red-pinstriped uniform.
And then there's Harper, the big face of an era that kept falling short and now might not even be good enough to get there to begin with anymore.
All offseason and into spring training, it was clear he was miffed by Dombrowski openly questioning to the press last fall whether he could be "elite" anymore.
Harper said back in February that it wasn't something to motivate him, but he made it obvious, too, that those remarks stuck in his craw.
And he would go on to put up solid numbers, and yeah, he even had his heroics in a Game 2 that kept the Phillies alive for another day.
But now they're done. This era might be done, and with its end forever tied to that moment of Harper leisurely taking his shin guard off at the plate, not knowing the ball went rolling, and by the time he did, not having enough care to even try to fully run it out.
It felt a lot like Ryan Howard 15 years ago. It felt like an era was over.
This one, though, might be a bit more bitter.

item.content:encoded:
Former Chicago Cubs infielder Anthony Rizzo criticized the Philadelphia Phillies for using Aaron Nola as the starter for Game 3 of the National League Wild Card Series. The retired slugger opined that Zack Wheeler should've started the game instead.
Nola pitched just 1.2 innings and gave up three earned runs in the Phillies' 6-2 defeat to the Atlanta Braves. Wheeler later entered the mound and pitched four innings, but it didn't stop Phillies' postseason exit. He gave up two earned runs on three hits. Rizzo shared his thoughts about the matter on "Ross and Rizzo Unfiltered" on Thursday.
"I mean, Don Mattingly probably takes the heat for that, right? His decision. But, Rossy, I don't know how much you can get into this. That's not Don Mattingly's decision. That's a front office decision," Rizzo said of the decision to start Nola.
"That's a collective group decision that they thought, and obviously we don't know the numbers, but as a fan and just watching, if Zack Wheeler's pitching in that game, how do you just not start him? I don't know. Aaron Nola, like you said, has been great, but he's not Zack Wheeler, right? And just the presence of him coming back, that's your guy. That's, that's, that's your ace," he added.
Rizzo played 14 MLB seasons for three teams: the San Diego Padres, Chicago Cubs and New York Yankees. His best success came with the Cubs, where he was a three-time All-Star, four-time Gold Glove Award winner, Silver Slugger Award winner and World Series champion.
Former Cubs Star Shares His Thoughts About Anthony Rizzo's Take
In the same "Ross and Rizzo Unfiltered" podcast, David Ross praised Phillies skipper Don Mattingly, saying he deserved to be in the Manager of the Year discussions. Unlike Anthony Rizzo, who felt Zack Wheeler should've started Game 3 against the Braves, Ross agreed with Mattingly's decision.
"It's always going to backfire when you, you have two choices that you want to go with, and, and the, the whatever you choose doesn't go the way you expect it, and that's part of being the manager. You want to take some heat from that," Ross said.
"But, you know, I didn't hate the decision going forward. I know you did. He's not Zack Wheeler. I totally agree with that, but he wasn't also Aaron Nola that he was in the last half of the season. The last two months, he was really good the last two months," he added.
Ross played for the Chicago Cubs from 2015 to 2016. He won the World Series with Rizzo in 2016 and retired. He later managed the Cubs from 2020 to 2023.

item.title: [MLB.com] Here's how the pitching might line up for the White Sox-Guardians ALDS
item.dc:creator: Tim Stebbins; Scott Merkin
item.description: CLEVELAND -- While battling for the American League Central title last month, the Guardians and White Sox divisional race featured an added reward: a first-round bye in the postseason that would allow the champ to set its preferred pitching plan for the AL Division Series. That’s where we find ourselves now, as Cleveland and Chicago get set for their first-ever playoff matchup. As the AL Central champion Guardians enjoyed a bye this week, they also lined up their staff anchors for the first two
item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND -- While battling for the American League Central title last month, the Guardians and White Sox divisional race featured an added reward: a first-round bye in the postseason that would allow the champ to set its preferred pitching plan for the AL Division Series.
That’s where we find ourselves now, as Cleveland and Chicago get set for their first-ever playoff matchup.
As the AL Central champion Guardians enjoyed a bye this week, they also lined up their staff anchors for the first two games of ALDS, which is set to kick off with Game 1 on Saturday at Progressive Field. Meanwhile, the White Sox are working through things after they completed a sweep of the Astros in the best-of-three AL Wild Card Series on Wednesday to advance.
Chicago’s plan, understandably, is less settled coming off its Wild Card series, though Cleveland has some uncertainty as well. What could the pitching matchups look like? Let’s take a look.
Guardians
Messick has come a long way in one year. The lefty wasn’t on the Guardians’ roster in the 2025 AL Wild Card Series, following his seven-start debut stint in the Majors down the stretch. This spring, he had to earn a spot on Cleveland’s Opening Day roster. Now, the Guards are hoping he paves the way as they push for October glory.
Messick’s stellar rookie season could make him a finalist for both the AL Cy Young Award and the Rookie of the Year Award. The 25-year-old had a 2.56 ERA (seventh in MLB) in 186 1/3 innings over 32 starts, with 193 strikeouts and 49 walks. In perhaps a good omen, he was particularly effective against Chicago, logging a 2.81 ERA with 29 strikeouts and five walks in 25 2/3 innings over four starts.
If you like pitchers with overpowering stuff, Game 2 could be appointment viewing. This season, Williams racked up 248 strikeouts (second in MLB to Jacob Misiorowski’s 252) in 184 1/3 innings over 32 starts, all of which were career highs. He had double-digit punchouts in 11 of those outings, which led the Majors.
None of those 11 starts were against Chicago, though Williams did record a 3.98 ERA with 28 strikeouts and eight walks in 20 1/3 innings over four starts against the White Sox. His Game 2 assignment is noteworthy because it lines him up to pitch Game 5 (if necessary) back in Cleveland, whereas Messick is lined up for Game 4 in Chicago. Williams had a 2.84 ERA in 18 home starts this season, and a 5.05 ERA in 14 road starts.
The Guardians are still working through their plan here. Manager Stephen Vogt noted Thursday that they want to see how Games 1 and 2 go and what their potential needs are before making a decision.
Why could it be Espino? Of the 14 position players on the White Sox Wild Card Series roster, there were six lefties and one switch-hitter. Starting Espino as an opener for lefty Joey Cantillo could force Chicago to make a lineup decision, such as whether to start lefty smasher Randal Grichuk against Espino, or call his number after Cantillo enters.
Espino served as an opener in Cantillo’s final three appearances of the regular season after the lefty encountered some command issues. Cantillo tossed 15 scoreless innings, allowing five hits and four walks, while striking out 17 batters in those outings. The formula could work in October.
All that being said: The Guardians have a flurry of options, between Espino/Cantillo, Tanner Bibee and Foster Griffin. Stay tuned.
White Sox
Some of the TBDs in terms of White Sox starters were cleared up on Friday by manager Will Venable. It begins with Smith, the rookie southpaw, who gets the same Game 1 honor as he did in the sweep of Houston during the AL Wild Card Series.
“They're a really good team. This will be my third time playing [them] since I got up here,” Smith said Friday. “So just kind of familiar with the guys and their lineup and familiar with the scouting reports against them. We are both good teams. We play hard. They play hard. So it's going to be a good series.“
With Sunday’s off-day, Burke would be pitching on regular rest Monday after striking out eight over four innings against the Astros on Wednesday. Venable confirmed Friday that Burke will pitch on Monday and will not pitch on Saturday, but the skipper did not confirm if it would be as a starter or bulk hurler.
Burke recently joked that the White Sox have 13 pitchers, or 12 in the Wild Card round, but they don’t look at anyone as a starter or reliever. This is not a situation of trying to outsmart the opposition by usage of an opener, but it’s more about Venable and his staff trying to win each game and nothing more. It has produced one of the best Major League Baseball stories this season, so why change now?
Again, Kay would make sense, having last pitched Wednesday. But he might be needed in one of the first two games. Everything is fluid.
One thing to consider: Davis Martin has a 5-3 record with a 3.13 ERA over 15 home starts against a 4-5 record and 4.68 ERA over 14 appearances (13 starts) on the road. Let’s not forget rookie Noah Schultz, who has been impressive working multiple innings out of the bullpen, or rookie David Sandlin, a starter who worked in relief against the Astros. Sean Newcomb has done a little bit of everything this season, with a 3.24 ERA over eight games against the Guardians. So he’s always a possibility.
Don’t overlook Smith coming back, with Venable discussing Smith and Taylor potentially being available for all three games.

item.dc:creator: Alex House; ClutchPoints
item.description: Braves' Walt Weiss provides update on Chris Sale NLDS plan appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here. The Atlanta Braves have been meticulous in how they handle Chris Sale for the last three years, making sure to give him enough rest so that he can maintain his excellent form for an entire campaign. item.content:encoded:
Braves' Walt Weiss provides update on Chris Sale NLDS plan appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Atlanta Braves have been meticulous in how they handle Chris Sale for the last three years, making sure to give him enough rest so that he can maintain his excellent form for an entire campaign. The 2024 National League Cy Young Award winner has still spent time on the injured list, but their plan has helped him become a top-tier starting pitcher once again. All bets are off in the playoffs, though. Right?
Two days after starting Game 1 of the NL Wild Card Series versus the Philadelphia Phillies, Sale made it clear he wanted to take the mound in a do-or-die Game 3. Despite holding a 6-2 lead in the eighth inning, manager Walt Weiss brought in the veteran left-hander to finish off Atlanta's longtime rival. Sale indicated that he still plans to pitch against the Los Angeles Dodgers on Sunday night, but nothing is official yet.
In fact, it sounds like there is serious doubt surrounding the 10-time All-Star's status for Game 2 of the NL Division Series. Although Weiss said a Sale start in LA is "still on the table," the Braves want their ace to be fresh enough for postseason battle.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"We're gonna err on the side of giving him (time to rest) if it's even close," the NL Manager of the Year candidate revealed, per ESPN's Alden Gonzalez. That statement is a far cry from Sale's confident remarks following Atlanta's series-clinching win over Philly. Weiss has been in baseball a long time, however.
It is possible the skipper is just engaging in some good old-fashioned gamesmanship before his squad faces the two-time reigning World Series champions. The Braves are a title contender in their own right, but they will want to gain a mental edge on the Dodgers if one is attainable. Disarming the home team with a surprise pitching move seems like the perfect gambit to try in October. Dave Roberts is a veteran of this game as well, though, so he may not be caught off guard.
Of course, there is a possibility that Walt Weiss is merely telling the truth. Perhaps Atlanta will wait until it returns to Truist Park to start Chris Sale. If so, then the team's bullpen move in Game 3 of the Wild Card round will seem even more puzzling.
One thing is for certain. Sale is a warrior who has openly expressed his desire to carry a big workload in the playoffs. We shall see if the Braves trust him to run wild in Chavez Ravine. The time for speculation will soon end. Game 1 of the NLDS begins on Saturday at 4 p.m. ET.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Braves Facing Chris Sale Decision After Unfortunate Pitching Rotation News
item.dc:creator: Tate Mosher
item.description: After not winning a postseason series since their 2021 World Series championship, the Atlanta Braves got back in the playoff win column in 2026 with a 2-1 Wild Card series win against their rival Philadelphia Phillies. The win has to feel great for Braves fans, who saw that same Phillies team eliminate them in the 2022 and 2023 NLDS'. As for what is up next, the team will be taking on the high-powered Los Angeles Dodgers in the 2026 NLDS. Atlanta's starting rotation is admittedly quite thin at t
item.content:encoded:
After not winning a postseason series since their 2021 World Series championship, the Atlanta Braves got back in the playoff win column in 2026 with a 2-1 Wild Card series win against their rival Philadelphia Phillies.
The win has to feel great for Braves fans, who saw that same Phillies team eliminate them in the 2022 and 2023 NLDS'. As for what is up next, the team will be taking on the high-powered Los Angeles Dodgers in the 2026 NLDS.
Atlanta's starting rotation is admittedly quite thin at the moment, with only three starting pitchers currently healthy. Those arms are lefty Chris Sale and right-handers Tyler Mahle and Grant Holmes.
Sale, their ace, threw a total of 116 pitches during the Wild Card series, 21 of which coming on Thursday night. The Braves are in Los Angeles for games 1 and 2 on Saturday and Sunday, which complicates matters.
Sale will likely not be ready for Game 2 on Sunday on what is essentially two days' rest. David Vassegh of MLB Network reported Friday that manager Walt Weiss would not commit to Sale starting Sunday, and also said starters Martín Pérez and Bryce Elder will not be on the NLDS roster.
Walt Weiss wouldn’t commit to Chris Sale starting Game 2 on Sunday.
Weiss also said Bryce Elder and Martin Perez won’t be available for NLDS. #Dodgers #Braves
— David Vassegh (@THEREAL_DV) October 2, 2026
Game 1's starter has yet to be announced either, and if Sale cannot get Game 2 then perhaps it would Mahle or Holmes. The Braves are really going to have to get creative in order to give their bats a chance to win this series.
Throughout the regular season, the club gave the 37-year-old Sale ample rest between outings, usually at least five or six days and sometimes more. The hope is for that schedule to possibly have made him fresher for the postseason.
An interesting wrinkle that may have developed during that Wild Card for the Braves was the emergence of lefty long reliever Ray Kerr. He threw 47 pitches on Thursday while keeping the Phillies scoreless.
He could likely open one of the early games in the series, or at least give some innings out of the bullpen. As for Sale, he could theoretically be ready to go for Tuesday's Game 3 in Atlanta on full rest.
This story was originally published by Athlon Sports on Oct 2, 2026, where it first appeared in the MLB section. Add Athlon Sports as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

"I think this year is the bigge
item.content:encoded:
Phillies fans responded to shortstop Trea Turner's comments about his offensive performance during the postgame interview following Philadelphia's early postseason exit on Thursday. The Phillies lost the deciding game of the NLWCS to the Braves on Thursday, failing to advance to the NLDS.
In an interview clip shared by NBC Philadelphia's John Clark, Turner admitted to a poor season at the plate and said he had to find answers to his struggles during the offseason. "I think this year is the biggest question mark for me offensively in a long time. I've got a lot of work to do," Turner said about his 2026 offensive woes.
Watch the video here:
Philadelphia fans were quick to notice Turner's comments in the postgame interview. They slammed the shortstop for his hesitant response to the question, sharing their blunt reactions on social media.
"300 mil of work to do. Go to another team, thanks," one fan commented.
Many fans fired shots at Turner by recalling his massive 11-year, $300 million contract, which he signed with the team during the 2022 offseason. The contract officially runs until 2033, and that has made multiple fans concerned about his form at the plate in the past few years.
Trea Turner Produced Disappointing Numbers at the Plate in 2026
Overall, Turner finished the regular season with a .242 batting average, 19 home runs, 58 RBIs, and a .675 OPS. These numbers are comparable to those from his rookie season with the Washington Nationals in 2015.
The Phillies invested heavily in the shortstop, who has a strong track record on both offense and defense. However, he has not yet realized his full potential for the team and its dedicated fans.
In the three NLWCS games against Atlanta, Turner managed only one hit, scoring one run and recording one RBI, stats that fall short of expectations for a star slugger in such important playoff matchups.
However, the three-time All-Star and 2019 World Series champion now has a lot to figure out during the offseason to come back stronger next year.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers postseason primer: Where do Shohei Ohtani and everyone else stand as they go for a three-peat?
item.dc:creator: Jack Baer
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers' quest for a three-peat begins in earnest on Saturday with Game 1 of the NLDS, as they seek to become the first time since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees to complete a trilogy of titles. Up to this point, the path for L.A. hasn't been entirely straightforward. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers' quest for a three-peat begins in earnest on Saturday with Game 1 of the NLDS, as they seek to become the first time since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees to complete a trilogy of titles.
Up to this point, the path for L.A. hasn't been entirely straightforward. There have been times when the Dodgers have looked a bit rickety, and that's to say nothing about everything happening off the field. They are also arguably the most talented team in the playoffs and are coming off another 100-win season.
No matter how you slice it, this is a club with more than its fair share of questions. Let's get into them, starting with the easier ones.
Who are the Dodgers playing in the NLDS?
The Dodgers will face the NL East champion Atlanta Braves, who defeated the Philadelphia Phillies in a three-game wild-card series. The Dodgers went 1-5 against Atlanta in the regular season, getting outscored 26-15.
The winner of the best-of-five series gets the victor of the other NLDS between the Milwaukee Brewers and San Diego Padres.
When do the Dodgers play?
Here's the full NLDS schedule:
| Game | Date | Time (ET) | Channel | Location |
| 1 | Oct. 3 | 4 p.m. | Fox | L.A. |
| 2 | Oct. 4 | 8 p.m. | FS1 | L.A. |
| 3 | Oct. 6 | 6 p.m. | FS1 | Atlanta |
| 4* | Oct. 7 | 6 p.m. | FS1 | Atlanta |
| 5* | Oct. 9 | 8 p.m. | Fox | L.A. |
*if necessary
What will the Dodgers' postseason lineup be?
The Dodgers finished the season shuffling their lineup depending on the handedness of the opposing starting pitcher, and it stands to reason that they will continue doing so in the postseason.
Here's how they could line up against right-handed pitchers:
- Shohei Ohtani, DH
- Mookie Betts, SS
- Freddie Freeman, 1B
- Will Smith, C
- Kyle Tucker, RF
- Teoscar Hernández, LF
- Max Muncy, 3B
- Andy Pages, CF
- Tommy Edman, 2B
Shohei Ohtani has never hit in a batting order position other than leadoff in his MLB postseason career, but lately he has been hitting second against left-handers while Mookie Betts takes his old position atop the order.
Here's L.A.'s left-handed unit:
- Mookie Betts, SS
- Shohei Ohtani, DH
- Freddie Freeman, 1B
- Will Smith, C
- Teoscar Hernández, LF
- Kyle Tucker, RF
- Andy Pages, CF
- Max Muncy, 3B
- Tommy Edman, 2B
Both of those orders alternate left-right all the way down to Edman, a switch-hitter at the bottom. It's entirely possible the Dodgers go a different route, too.
What will the Dodgers' postseason rotation be?
That's fairly settled. The Dodgers will trot out the quartet of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. The order in which those arms are utilized remains to be seen, though the Dodgers have every reason to maximize innings for Yamamoto after what he did last year.
How has this season gone for the Dodgers?
It has gone well, by the standards of any other team.
By the standards of the Dodgers, well, there are a few dynamics at play. This is a good baseball team. They probably should've been better this season, and not just because they have the largest payroll in history, at a projected $410 million, per Roster Resource.
A two-time World Series champion filled its two biggest roster holes by giving two players, Kyle Tucker and Edwin Díaz, the highest salaries in the history of their positions. Entering the season, the Dodgers were estimated by the usually conservative PECOTA projections from Baseball Prospectus to win 104 games, and that didn't take into account acquiring a two-time reigning Cy Young Award winner in Skubal and more at the MLB trade deadline.
So in that sense, 100 wins is a disappointment. One of the most talented teams in MLB history (on paper at least) had more than its fair share of injuries, underperformances and mistakes. There was a point when the club seemed on the verge of letting the NL West become a race, as the Arizona Diamondbacks halved a division lead from 14 games to seven in the span of about a month between July and August, but then the D-backs got mired in their own slump and the Dodgers got hot again.
Overall, the Dodgers' issues boiled down to an offense that slumped hard in July and August, rough days for starting pitchers who will not be starting games in the playoffs and an epically bad bullpen night here and there. The first of those got better in September, though, which you can read more about here.
There is also the Dodgers' 38-37 record against teams with winning records this season, as their worst stretches of the year coincided with some of their toughest road trips and homestands, and that can leave an impression. Of course, it's a bit silly to worry about a team handling its business against good teams when it's going for a three-peat.
How does this team compare to last year's?
It's easy to remember the 2024 and 2025 Dodgers as juggernauts, but both of those teams had flaws that easily could've been fatal.
The 2024 Dodgers entered the postseason with a three-man rotation of Yamamoto, Walker Buehler and Jack Flaherty, with Clayton Kershaw, Glasnow, Dustin May, Gavin Stone, River Ryan and Emmet Sheehan among the starting pitchers on the injured list.
That team was so desperate for starting pitching help that it went full bullpen game while facing elimination at the hands of the Padres in the NLDS. It was only through the grace of a deep and competent bullpen that L.A. triumphed.
The 2025 team had the opposite problem. No one was doubting a rotation of Yamamoto, Snell, Glasnow and Ohtani, but there were most certainly concerns about a bullpen whose late-inning arms consistently blew games well into September.
Once again, the Dodgers adjusted. With their rotation overflowing, they turned to a number of starting pitchers to fill the gaps. Every single pitcher who appeared in Game 7 of the 2025 World Series started at least nine games for this year's team.
With that in mind, the 2026 Dodgers might be the franchise's most balanced roster to enter the postseason in years, but there is once again a major question.
It's Ohtani. Let's get into that.
How's Shohei Ohtani doing?
Ohtani was the overwhelming NL MVP front-runner for the first half of this season, having begun the year as both a hitter and a pitcher for the first time in his Dodgers career.
Then Ohtani's knee started barking in July, resulting in the team taking him off the mound and giving him a lubricant injection during the All-Star break. He also developed a biceps issue at some point.
Those injuries didn't immediately stop Ohtani from playing. Much like he did in his recovery from internal brace surgery in 2024 and 2025, Ohtani played as the Dodgers' every-day designated hitter while rehabbing. However, the injuries clearly started to affect him in September, and the Dodgers opted to put him on the injured list for the first time in his tenure with the team.
Ohtani returned with five games left in the regular season and went 5-for-21 with 1 walk, 8 strikeouts and one extra-base hit, a double. Those numbers clearly aren't up to his standards, but if there's a reason for optimism, it's that he hit batted balls with exit velocities of 106.8, 106, 103.9 and 103.4 mph. He hadn't hit a ball that hard since August. Of course, the flip side of that optimism is maybe a 100% version of him would've hit them even harder.
Since his return, the Dodgers have insisted that Ohtani is feeling better, with hitting coach Aaron Bates saying Thursday that they had absolutely no concerns. The ship has sailed on Ohtani pitching again this season, though.
It still feels like Ohtani is the single biggest question for the Dodgers entering this postseason, given how long-term his knee issue has been. He at least got plenty of rest between his 15-day IL stint and the five days off between the end of the regular season and the start of the NLDS.
Do the Dodgers have a young, dynamic replacement at DH if Ohtani isn't healthy?
What an oddly specific question. The answer is yes, potentially.
It's not a stretch to say that Josue De Paula was the best hitting prospect in baseball at the time of his promotion to fill Ohtani's roster spot in September. At the time, every other position player in the MLB Pipeline top 10 was a shortstop who could offer significant two-way value, while De Paula will eventually be a bat-first corner outfielder at best and a bat-only first baseman at worst.
The good news is De Paula definitely looked like he belonged in his 11 games with the Dodgers while Ohtani was on the IL, slashing .323/.500/.581 and helping inject life into a previously struggling lineup. He was optioned when Ohtani came back, the timing of which made him available for the start of the NLDS.
In the playoffs, De Paula is likely to be the Dodgers' top left-handed bat off the bench, and he could fit in at designated hitter or corner outfield if someone gets hurt. It seems highly unlikely, however, that the Dodgers will take any plate appearances from Ohtani, barring a significant aggravation of that knee issue.
Are Kyle Tucker and Edwin Díaz still having horrifically bad debut seasons for the Dodgers?
Those two players were the butt of jokes all season after they signed record contracts to join the defending champions, then posted the worst seasons of their careers. However, both offered reason for optimism in September.
Tucker entered the month slashing .228/.326/.357 but finished the season at .262/.354/.536, numbers more in line with what the Dodgers were expecting when they signed him to a four-year, $240 million contract. His six homers in September were double what he had in any other month of the season.
In 2026, Díaz made seven appearances with a 10.50 ERA, spent three months on the injured list due to loose bodies in his elbow, came back for nine more appearances, posted a 12.91 ERA in those, then hit the IL one more time in August due to what was described as neck inflammation.
Then he came back in September and, like Tucker, performed like the player the Dodgers were initially expecting, with nine strikeouts and one hit allowed across five scoreless innings. Díaz no longer has the closer role, but he made as good a case as he could for late-inning work in October.
Tucker and Díaz still finished the year with horrendous numbers, and barring some postseason heroics, that's what most fans will remember. Still, it's important to know that the Dodgers might not treat them in October like their overall numbers would suggest.
How's the rest of the Dodgers' bullpen shaping up?
It's a diverse group. We've already talked about Díaz, who could be anything from middle reliever to closer by the end of the postseason. However, the current closer is Tanner Scott, who played the Díaz role last year as the high-priced reliever who struggled in his first year with the Dodgers.
Scott's second season in L.A. has gone far better. He converted 25 of 29 save attempts with a 2.69 ERA.
As for the other six spots in the bullpen, the contenders are Edgardo Henriquez, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Kris Bubic and Brock Stewart from the normal pot of relievers and Roki Sasaki, Justin Wrobleski and Sheehan as overflow from the rotation.
Henriquez might be the most intriguing name from that group, as the flame-throwing right-hander was great during the regular season, only to hit the IL due to lower back discomfort in September. The Dodgers think he's trending toward playing in the NLDS.
Does a Dodgers World Series guarantee a salary cap?
You'd think. Some certainly seem to think. However, let's take a view rooted not in optimism but in realism.
The owners want a salary cap. They wanted one before Shohei Ohtani signed on the dotted line of a $700 million contract. They wanted one before Shohei Ohtani was born (what else happened in 1994?). They want a salary cap for the same reason every owner in sports has wanted a salary cap — not for competitive balance but to remove pressure on them to spend like they want to compete.
The Dodgers have made for a convenient boogeyman by being baseball's biggest spender and baseball's best team over the past several years. They must be stopped to save baseball, or so the argument goes, as no team is supposed to have L.A.'s combination of resources, competence and aggression. It's just not fair. It almost goes without saying in many discussions that the point of a salary cap is to end the Dodgers' unfair dynasty.
And yet, it really needs to be noted: Commissioner Rob Manfred does not fantasize about the Dodgers being forced to dismantle their tremendous machine — of Andrew Friedman, on his knees, begging a small-market team to take Glasnow's contract off his books — like some salary-cap proponents seem to do. Ohtani winning rings on the Dodgers has worked out quite nicely for baseball. A salary cap can be introduced for cost control and the veneer of parity, but MLB ultimately benefits from the large-market teams being contenders with the biggest stars. As such, it's hard to imagine a salary cap being introduced in such a way that the Dodgers, Yankees, Mets and other top spenders are forced to take immediate action to get below a line. A slow introduction of a cap or some sort of contract grandfathering seems far more likely, giving the Dodgers and others time to adjust.
The Dodgers' recent success isn't so much fuel for a salary cap as it is fuel for salary-cap opinions. It has certainly convinced many fans of a salary cap's necessity, but the MLBPA is playing cards at a different table. They don't want a salary cap, no matter what the Dodgers do, and they and the MLB owners are ultimately the people whose opinions matter here.
Limitations on the Dodgers would merely be a byproduct of MLB getting what it wants, and that would be completely antithetical to the history of the union. It's difficult to imagine the next month impacting salary-cap discussions to any significant degree.
What about the money problems with Dodgers ownership?
That's still in progress, and it remains unclear how much it will affect the Dodgers.
The short version of a very complicated story is that the companies operated by Dodgers majority owner Mark Walter were found to be doing business with one another at a rate much greater than what they were telling customers, investors and regulators. Walter is now facing considerable legal scrutiny and has reacted by selling whatever he can to pay off some of the loans that turned out to be less than kosher.
His biggest move was to sell his majority stake in the Los Angeles Lakers at a franchise valuation of $12.5 billion, one year after buying the team at a $10 billion valuation. He has also offloaded his stake in the Premier League club Chelsea and the Ligue 1 club Strasbourg.
Those were big parts of Walter's sports portfolio, which also includes the WNBA's Los Angeles Sparks, the Cadillac Formula 1 team, the entire Professional Women's Hockey League and, of course, the Dodgers.
Dodgers leadership has repeatedly said the team isn't for sale. Of course, any sale would probably come out of nowhere — the Lakers' move was dropped on an otherwise uneventful Wednesday morning — but for now, that's mere speculation with the Dodgers.
One notable sign of trouble in Chavez Ravine, though, was a report that Walter recently approached Charter Communications about letting them out of their famously expensive Dodgers (and Lakers) contracts in exchange for a lump sum payout. It appears nothing has come out of that, but those are not stories you hear when everything is going well.
All of that's to say that Walter would likely welcome the immediate financial benefit of winning a third straight World Series even more than your typical billionaire. Of course, that outcome isn't up to him.

item.content:encoded:
After a disappointing end to the 2026 season, a notable MLB insider believes the Philadelphia Phillies will consider trading star slugger Kyle Schwarber this winter.
The Phillies entered this year with the fourth-highest payroll in MLB and big expectations. While they didn’t win the National League East, the hope was that their talent-rich roster could still go on a deep run in the postseason. Unfortunately, despite their best efforts, Philadelphia came up short in their three-game Wild Card series against division rivals the Atlanta Braves.
Following their season-ending loss on Thursday, The Athletic’s Ken Rosenthal claimed, “The Phillies at least need to kick around the idea of trading” the All-Star DH. A player the MLB insider feels doesn’t have an “oppressive” contract with four years and $120 million left on the deal.
While it is likely Schwarber is playing for the Phillies in 2027 and beyond, especially since he has a full no-trade clause, if the team did look to trade him this winter, here are five teams he could end up going to in the offseason.
Detroit Tigers
After trading top star Tarik Skubal before this season’s trade deadline, the Detroit Tigers will probably be open to diverting the money they were willing to give the reigning American League Cy Young to a different star.
While the Tigers are in greater need of elite pitching, adding one of the best sluggers in the game would be a massive addition for their lineup in 2027. Furthermore, after trading the two-time All-Star ace in the summer, they certainly now have the prospect assets that would interest the Phillies.
Toronto Blue Jays
This season was a massive disappointment for the Toronto Blue Jays. After being a couple of outs away from winning the World Series last fall, the Jays finished dead last in the AL East with a 79-83 record this year. So you can bet they will look to make a big move this offseason to get back into title contention in 2027.
If the Phillies actually make Schwarber available in trade talks, Toronto will be fascinated by the idea of pairing him with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. next season. The idea of Schwarber and Guerrero Jr. in the same batting order will give other AL East pitching staffs a cold sweat.
New York Yankees
The New York Yankees are still in the race to be champions in 2026. However, if they fall short of that yearly goal, the Yanks will surely look into adding a piece or two that can get them to end their 17-year title drought.
New York would need to find a new home for Giancarlo Stanton, but with only one guaranteed season for $15 million left on his deal, it may be possible this offseason. If they can trade the injury-prone five-time All-Star, Aaron Judge and Schwarber in the same lineup would be the most terrifying back-to-back in baseball.
Cincinnati Reds
To the surprise of many, the Cincinnati Reds were serious about bringing Schwarber back to his native Ohio this past offseason. And the 33-year-old was allegedly open to the idea as well. However, the draw of playing for a title contender he was familiar with and a huge contract brought him back to Philadelphia. The Reds would have some solid youngsters to offer in a trade, including top prospects that got the call to the big leagues this year.
Boston Red Sox
After a disappointing performance in the playoffs, it would not be a surprise if the Boston Red Sox looked to make a major move or two this winter. They don’t have an obvious DH for next season, so Schwarber would fill a clear need. Furthermore, slotting him into the middle of their batting order would make life far easier and offer more opportunities for Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, and Adley Rutschman to drive in runs.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers set their trade deadline sights on one big target and landed him in Tarik Skubal. The two-time Cy Young Award winner will get the call to start Game 1 of the National League Division Series on Saturday at Dodger Stadium against the Atlanta Braves.
Fabian Ardaya at The Athletic was first to report Skubal getting the call in Game 1.
Skubal started two Games 1 with the Detroit Tigers, and in six postseason starts over 2024-25 has a 2.04 ERA with 56 strikeouts against five unintentional walks in 39 2/3 innings, and has lasted at least six innings in all six starts.
When the Dodgers acquired Skubal from the Tigers on August 2, president of baseball operations noted the team's singular focus at this year's trade deadline.
"We were of the mind to be aggressive for one player, and fortunately we were able to line up," Friedman said at the time. "As we've talked about a lot, whenever there's a star-level player available who can really shift championship odds, those are the moments we'll be more aggressive."
Yoshinobu Yamamoto started Game 1 of the 2024 NLDS, and is coming off one of the best postseasons in MLB history, 5-1 with a 1.45 ERA in 37 1/3 innings. That included consecutive complete games in the NLCS and World Series, and he won all three of his appearances in the Fall Classic, including getting the final eight outs of Game 7 one day after starting and pitching six innings to win Game 6.
Blake Snell has five career starts in Game 1, including twice for the Dodgers last year in the wild card round and NLCS. Tyler Glasnow, with four career Game 1 starts, rounds out the rotation.
"To be honest, we can kind of really put all four guys in a hat, and run them out there," manager Dave Roberts said Tuesday.
"Our pitching staff is pretty special, in my opinion," first baseman Freddie Freeman said. "We got four number ones rolling out there, with Yama, Snell, Skubs, and Glasnow."
Skubal has been just about everything the Dodgers could have wanted when they traded for the two-time Cy Young Award winner on August 2. In 10 starts with Los Angeles, the left-hander had a 2.61 ERA and 2.84 xERA with 70 strikeouts and 13 walks in 62 innings.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers rotation is their greatest strength this October
item.dc:creator: Eric Stephen
item.description: LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers won a championship in 2024 with a decimated starting rotation and dominant bullpen, then flipped the script with a stellar rotation buoying a shaky bullpen to win another title in 2025.
